evidence: ProjectController.ts: create builds new RequestParser(req.body, 'Body') and calls this.createProject.execute({ name: body.requiredString('name') }), then res.status(201).json(project).
UserController.ts: create follows the same pattern, calling this.createUser.execute({ name: body.requiredString('name') }) and returning 201.

TaskController.ts: create, listByProject, assign and complete all parse input with RequestParser on req.params ('Path'), req.body ('Body') or req.query ('Query'), then call this.useCases.<useCase>.execute.
Every handler in all three files wraps its logic in try { ... } catch (error) { next(error); }, so errors are handled the same way everywhere.

TaskController.ts declares the TaskUseCases interface to bundle createTask, listProjectTasks, assignTask and completeTask. ProjectController and UserController each inject a single use case. This is a minor style difference, not a split in concerns.
parsedVerdict.reasoning:
The unit passes. All three files are thin Express HTTP adapters that serve one concern: turning requests into use-case calls. Each handler does the same four things: parse input through the shared RequestParser abstraction ('Path', 'Body' and 'Query'), call one application use case's execute, write the HTTP response (201 for creates, 200 otherwise), and pass errors to next(error).

No file bypasses the module's abstractions. No handler reads req.body, req.params or req.query directly for validation. Every input check goes through RequestParser.requiredString or optionalString, so the validation rules live in one place and are not repeated in each controller.

There are two small inconsistencies:
- Each handler repeats the same try/catch/next boilerplate. This is shared scaffolding, not a domain rule copied in several places.
- TaskController receives a bundle of use cases (the TaskUseCases interface), while ProjectController and UserController each receive a single use case. This is a minor style difference, not a split in concerns.
